| [LIT-097](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-097.md) v3 | The Extended Mind | Clark & Chalmers (1998), DOI-10.1093/analys/58.1.7. The paper argues from a functionalist parity claim that a process or standing state which would count as cognitive if it happened in the head counts as cognitive when an external resource carries it, provided the resource is actively coupled to the organism here and now. Otto's notebook entry is its example of such a standing belief. From this it infers, in one paragraph, that the self extends too. The four "criteria" for a coupled resource (constancy, direct availability, automatic endorsement, and the admittedly "arguable" past conscious endorsement) are offered as the features that make the paradigm case clear. The paper explicitly says they are not necessary and sufficient conditions. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-180](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-180.md)); it is worth reading as the source text of the extended-mind thesis, and it is short. Its constitutive conclusion follows from a role-functionalism about belief and a parity principle that the paper states rather than defends, so a reader should take it as the origin of the debate and not as its settlement. |
| [LIT-207](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-207.md) v2 | Talkative AI and the fiction of artificial minds | Roberts (2026), DOI-10.1007/s11098-026-02560-8. Roberts argues that users can nonetheless engage chatbots through make-believe, as a new kind of fictional character that is interactive, co-constructed, self-involving and blended with the real world. In the four-deck gambling task, 10 controls and 6 ventromedial prefrontal patients were tracked on choices, anticipatory skin-conductance responses and verbal reports. The headline that controls chose well and responded to risky decks "before they knew" is only partly carried by the statistics: in the pre-hunch period the controls' preference for the good decks was not significant (note 9), and the reported SCR effect there is a group-by-period interaction, not a bad-versus-good-deck difference (note 8). | [LIT-384](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-384.md) | The somatic marker hypothesis and the possible functions of the prefrontal cortex | Damasio (1996), DOI-10.1098/rstb.1996.0125. States the somatic marker hypothesis: ventromedial prefrontal cortex holds learned links between classes of situation and the body states (emotions) that went with them; when a situation recurs, those states are re-enacted, through the body or through an "as if" loop in somatosensory cortex, and mark imagined option-outcome pairs as good or bad, overtly as a feeling or covertly as a bias, so that reasoning works over a pruned space. Evidence summarised: ventromedial patients with intact intellect decide badly in life, lack skin-conductance responses to emotive pictures, and in the gambling task keep choosing the losing decks and show no anticipatory responses. | Active — read in full 2026-10-01 ([NOTE-332](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-332.md)); worth reading as the shortest statement of the somatic marker hypothesis by its author, with the evidence it then rested on. It is a hypothesis paper: the mechanism (ventromedial prefrontal linkages that re-enact body states, by a "body loop" or an "as if body loop", which then mark options good or bad) is stated, not shown, and the evidence it reports is lesion and skin-conductance work summarised from other papers, without numbers. Its strongest piece, that ventromedial patients lack anticipatory skin-conductance responses in the gambling task while responding normally to the losses themselves, is reported here in one paragraph; the 1997 Science report filed alongside it is the place to see that result. Whether the account is true is not this note's question. |

| [LIT-566](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-566.md) | Defining Agency: Individuality, Normativity, Asymmetry, and Spatio-temporality in Action | Barandiaran, Di Paolo & Rohde (2009), Adaptive Behavior 17(5):367–386. Three conditions are jointly necessary and sufficient for minimal agency: the system defines its own individuality, it is the active source of modulations of its coupling with the environment (interactional asymmetry), and it regulates that coupling by norms it generates (normativity). Generatively, an agent is an open autonomous system (a precarious network of mutually enabling processes) that adaptively modulates its coupling so as to maintain some of its constituent processes. Minimal life satisfies this; life is sufficient for agency but not necessary. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-458](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-458.md)), from the authors' own deposit of the accepted text. Worth reading as the standard organizational definition of minimal agency, and as the clearest statement that an agent is not the same thing as an individual. Individuality is one of three conditions, with interactional asymmetry and normativity; it is a precondition for the other two and is not sufficient for agency. The generative definition: an agent is an autonomous organization that adaptively regulates its coupling with its environment and contributes to sustaining itself as a consequence. The paper rejects statistical and energetic measures of asymmetry as sufficient, and says systems optimising an externally fixed function should not be treated as models of agency. |

| [LIT-601](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-601.md) | The Haken–Kelso–Bunz (HKB) model: from matter to movement to mind | Kelso (2021), Biological Cybernetics 115(4):305–322, a 60th-anniversary retrospective. HKB models bimanual coordination by the relative phase φ, with dφ/dt = −a sin φ − 2b sin 2φ and potential V = −a cos φ − b cos 2φ: both in-phase and anti-phase are stable for b/a > 1/4, and anti-phase loses stability below it, as observed when movement frequency rises. The same dynamics is reported within a body, between people and with machines, and in brain activity. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-467](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-467.md)), from the free-to-read publisher PDF. Worth reading as Kelso's own short statement of coordination dynamics: the HKB order-parameter equation for relative phase, its stochastic and symmetry-breaking extensions, metastability as relative coordination, the generalized HKB–Kuramoto model, and the claim that one coordination dynamics holds within and between people. It gives no test that tells a produced boundary from an imposed one, and it says a multicellular organism is not itself autopoietic. Its intrinsic teleology is value for the organism, though one paragraph runs on to a right to life. |
| [LIT-1027](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1027.md) | Genealogies of organizational closure: from logical paradox to mind in life | Rubin, Roli, Stano and Damiano (2026), Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence 9. A genealogy of the notions of closure from mathematical logic, cybernetics, systems theory, thermodynamics, relational biology and the biology of cognition, showing that each closes a different thing. It then argues that closure is a circular organization of efficient causes, distinct from feedback, self-organization and catalytic cycles and not exhaustively describable as a state-determined syntactic procedure, and that current AI approximates closure without instantiating it. | Active — read in full 2026-10-13 ([NOTE-727](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-727.md)) from the publisher's open-access PDF under CC BY (frontiersin.org/journals/artificial-intelligence/articles/10.3389/frai.2026.1806435/pdf). Registered from the 2026-10-13 exchange on meaning operators and selfhood (the workbench entry of 2026-10-13, 21:29). Worth reading as a map of what each notion of closure closes (information, operations, efficient causes, constraints, catalysts) and where each came from. Its thesis, closure as circular production of efficient causes that no state-determined syntactic description captures, supports [CLAIM-288](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-288.md) and goes beyond it: a system whose objectives its own processes revise is still, on this account, not closed. It gives no test for [QUESTION-086](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-086.md), and its non-computability claim rests on Rosen, unassessed. |
| [LIT-1054](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1054.md) | On Distinguishing Epistemic from Pragmatic Action | Kirsh and Maglio (1994), Cognitive Science 18(4). Kirsh and Maglio define an epistemic action as a physical action whose primary function is to reduce the space, time or unreliability of the agent's own mental computation, and argue from Tetris keystroke data that players rotate and translate pieces for that reason: zoids are rotated more than plan-then-act would need, rotation starts within a few hundred milliseconds of a zoid appearing, and a translate-to-wall check is used more the higher the drop. The computational saving is argued, not measured: physical rotation of 90° takes as little as 100 ms against an estimated 800–1200 ms mentally (a three-player pilot), and fewer attentional probes and less working memory are needed. The trade is physical action in place of internal computation at the moment of use, not precomputation or caching; the paper explicitly sets it against caching and chunking accounts of skill, and mentions amortized complexity only in passing for everyday cases such as sorting bolts before assembly. It says the choice fits a Stigler-style cost–benefit model in outline but that such models fail in detail, because an epistemic action's value depends on the particular internal computation it serves. | Active — read in full 2026-10-15 from the scan of the published article (Cognitive Science 18(4), pp. 513–549) that David Kirsh posts on his UCSD publications page (adrenaline.ucsd.edu/kirsh/Articles/CogsciJournal/DistinguishingEpi_prag.pdf); the Wiley open-access PDF that OpenAlex lists refused requests from this environment. Worth reading as the founding definition of epistemic action: a physical action whose primary function is to reduce the space, time or unreliability of the agent's own mental computation, argued from Tetris players' extra and early rotations (rotation under way by 400–600 ms, physical rotation in as little as 100 ms against an estimated 800–1200 ms mentally) and a translate-to-wall check used more for higher drops. For [QUESTION-095](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-095.md) it shows offloading at the moment of use, not precomputation: it sets itself against caching accounts of skill, mentions amortized complexity only in a parenthesis about sorting bolts, gives no formal cost model, and says simple cost–benefit models fail because an epistemic action's value depends on the computation it serves. For [TERM-055](../../../record/terms.d/TERM-055.md) it is a case of raising availability during the deadline, not before the request; for [CLAIM-303](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-303.md) it has a single use and no upkeep, so it bears only on the general shape of the trade. |
| [LIT-1057](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1057.md) | Adapting the Environment Instead of Oneself | Kirsh (1996), Adaptive Behavior 4(3–4). A conceptual paper. It models a task as a directed graph of states and actions with a cost metric on transitions, and classifies how an agent can improve its payoff by actions external to the task: pruning hard initial states, routine maintenance, scouting ahead, tools (which change the graph), and actions that make a space more "cognitively congenial" (which leave the graph intact and reduce mental operations). It names amortization once, as a parenthetical gloss on chimps leaving nut-cracking stones in place, and gives an investment rule for maintenance (future benefit against present cost times an "interest factor" for risk) in words only. There is no cost model with reuse frequency, retrieval cost or staleness; mental cost lies outside the graph, and the paper says there is "no general theory" of congeniality. The empirical figures are unpublished pilot results. | Active — read in full 2026-10-15 from a scan of the published article (Adaptive Behavior 4(3/4), pp. 415–452) that the author posts on his UCSD laboratory server (interactivity.ucsd.edu/articles/Adaptive/Adapting_env_00.pdf), text by OCR and cross-checked against the author's HTML version in the same directory; the PhilArchive copy refused automated requests and was not used. Worth reading as the distributed-cognition statement of environment redesign as a change to a task's state graph or to its "cognitive congeniality", with routine maintenance (keep things where they are expected so that search is unnecessary, against objects' tendency to scatter) and an investment rule for doing work before it is needed. For [QUESTION-095](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-095.md) it shows that "amortize the cost of search" is a single parenthetical about chimps leaving nut-cracking stones in place, not developed; that the graph prices only physical transitions, so retrieval and mental cost fall outside the formalism by the paper's own account; and that the nearest thing to a cost model is a verbal "interest factor" whose footnote names the risks that the result will not be used and that the change will not still be present, with no reuse frequency, retrieval cost, staleness of a result or query predictability. Its most usable point is that labour cost varies over time, so work should be done when it is cheap, which is the cockpit's rationale. It does not cite Tarjan (that is Kirsh 1995, [LIT-1076](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1076.md)), and its value-of-information example changes outcome probabilities rather than pricing a choice made after looking. For [CASE-085](../../../record/cases.d/CASE-085.md) it supports the labelled-compartment and standard-layout counterfactuals and their upkeep by the agent, a mechanism or the group, and says nothing on search cost, deadlines or when to stop searching. |
| [LIT-1059](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1059.md) | Cognitive Offloading | Risko and Gilbert (2016), TICS 20(9). A short review that defines cognitive offloading as physical action that changes a task's information-processing requirements to reduce cognitive demand, splits it into offloading onto the body and into the world, and proposes a metacognitive model: whether people offload is a strategy choice driven by their evaluation of internal versus extended strategies, which tracks objective internal demand but can be wrong, and offloading in turn changes both memory and those evaluations. The evidence is a handful of choice/no-choice studies, summarised qualitatively; the review reports no effect sizes and no formal account of costs. It names costs (memory for offloaded content, GPS-impaired spatial memory, photo-taking impairment, automation complacency and bias, skill decay, inflated self-knowledge, a self-reinforcing drift toward external reliance). It does not frame offloading as computation reused over time, and says nothing about how often an offloaded result is used. | Active — read in full 2026-10-15 from the authors' manuscript in UCL Discovery (discovery.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/1508770/1/gilbert_TiCS_OFFLOADING_RPS.pdf, 37 pp.; the typeset Elsevier version, its Trends box and its Outstanding Questions box were not seen). Worth reading as the standard definition of cognitive offloading ("the use of physical action to alter the information processing requirements of a task in order to reduce cognitive demand"), its split into onto-the-body and into-the-world, and a metacognitive model in which the choice to offload follows beliefs about internal versus extended strategies, tracks objective demand but can be wrong, and feeds back through lost memory and changed confidence into a drift toward external reliance. It reports no effect sizes and gives no cost formalism. For [QUESTION-095](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-095.md) it does not supply the retrieval-as-amortized-computation account; it adds that offloading shifts remembering "what" to remembering "where", that people offload where it gives nothing (about 40% at ceiling load), so when it pays and when people do it come apart, and that automation bias is the nearest thing to the staleness cost. For [CLAIM-303](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-303.md) it fits the direction (more is offloaded as the later internal cost rises) but says nothing about reuse count, and shows that offloading itself lowers internal capacity, which the claim's fixed ledger leaves out. |
| [LIT-1060](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1060.md) | Cognition in the Wild | Hutchins (1995), MIT Press. A study of navigation aboard a ship, arguing that cognitive processes are distributed across people, artifacts and their organization, and that the unit of analysis is the functional system. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-15, not read. Registered from the exchange of 2026-10-14 on prompting, epistemic memory and retrieval (the workbench entry of 2026-10-15). No NOTE is filed, and it stays Unavailable until it is read, not on merit. Looked for a lawful full text on 2026-10-15 and found none. Unpaywall and OpenAlex report it open access (green) on the strength of a single repository record at the University of Ljubljana (repozitorij.uni-lj.si/IzpisGradiva.php?id=44611, no PDF URL given); that record returns HTTP 410 with "Gradivo ne obstaja" (the item does not exist), and the Internet Archive has no capture of it, so the OA flag is stale. OpenAlex marks the MIT Press location itself as not open access, Crossref carries no licence for the DOI, and Semantic Scholar reports it closed. MIT Press Direct (direct.mit.edu/books/monograph/4604/Cognition-in-the-Wild, reached through the DOI) and the MIT Press catalogue page both returned 403 behind a Cloudflare challenge, the Internet Archive holds no capture of either, and a web search found only paid editions and library records and no sign that MIT Press has made the title open access. Hutchins's own UCSD site (pages.ucsd.edu/~ehutchins/citw.html) posts the book's Introduction in full (about 3,000 words: how the study began, the critique of an ideational, inside-the-head view of culture and cognition, and a chapter-by-chapter outline), but nothing else from the book. hci.ucsd.edu/hutchins/ is a JavaScript shell with no documents. No shadow library, Internet Archive lending copy or third-party upload was used. The Introduction states the move the record cites it for. It does not argue for it. It says Hutchins will "move the boundaries of the cognitive unit of analysis out beyond the skin of the individual person and treat the navigation team as a cognitive and computational system", that "local functional systems composed of a person in interaction with a tool have cognitive properties that are radically different from the cognitive properties of the person alone" (chapter 3), and that "Depending on their organization, groups must have cognitive properties that are not predictable from a knowledge of the properties of the individuals in the group" (chapter 4 takes the team as a whole). Hutchins's "How a cockpit remembers its speeds" (Cognitive Science 19(3), 1995, pp. 265–288, DOI 10.1207/s15516709cog1903_1) has lawful copies: the author posts the typeset article (pages.ucsd.edu/~ehutchins/documents/CockpitSpeeds.pdf, 24 pp., fetched 2026-10-15), and Unpaywall, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar list Wiley's free publisher PDF (bronze; onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdfdirect/10.1207/s15516709cog1903_1, which returned 403 to this environment). It is not registered, and it is the reading available now for [QUESTION-101](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-101.md). |

| [LIT-1066](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1066.md) | How a Cockpit Remembers Its Speeds | Hutchins (1995), Cognitive Science 19(3), 265–288. A task analysis of how a two-pilot airliner cockpit "remembers" approach speeds: computed early from a speed-card booklet indexed by gross weight, passed across speech to bugs on the airspeed indicators, and used minutes later as a judgement of spatial adjacency. The memory is a property of the functional system, "not made primarily of pilot memory", though pilot memory is involved. Stylized and unmeasured, for an anticipated, invariant task. | Active — read in full 2026-10-15 from the author's posted copy, a scan of the published article (Cognitive Science 19(3), pp. 265–288) at pages.ucsd.edu/~ehutchins/documents/CockpitSpeeds.pdf. Worth reading as the compact statement of distributed cognition's method, a cockpit treated as a cognitive system whose representations can be observed, and as the source of the speed-bug argument: setting the day's speeds as bugs on the airspeed indicator does not improve any pilot's memory but turns recall and scale-reading into a judgment of spatial proximity, so the memory "has now become a property of a larger system". For [QUESTION-101](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-101.md) and [CLAIM-296](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-296.md) it shows, by task analysis and not by measurement, a change of arrangement alone changing what the system can do; the retrieval cue (displayed gross weight, the needle nearing a bug) supplied by the environment; and the work of retrieval moved to a quiet phase 25 to 30 minutes ahead of use, which the record's deadline does not yet represent. It narrows them: its task is anticipated, mandated and invariant, it analyses only success, and it says nothing about search for one item among many under a deadline, which is [CASE-085](../../../record/cases.d/CASE-085.md)'s situation. |
| [LIT-1075](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1075.md) | Deictic codes for the embodiment of cognition | Ballard, Hayhoe, Pook and Rao (1997), BBS 20(4). At about a third of a second, the time scale of a saccade, the article models fixation as a pointer that binds a variable in a behavioural program to a place in the world, so that what is bound is only the task-relevant feature, fetched just before use. In a block-copying task subjects looked back at the model about 1.3 times per block on average, the commonest cycle being two looks per block (one apparently for colour, one for position), and chose this slowest, lowest-memory strategy (about 3 s a block, against about 1.5 s for copying from memory) though told to be fast; separating model and copy by 70° cut looks to 1.0 per block, and one-colour patterns that could be chunked cut them to 0.7. The authors read this as working memory having a "carrying cost" that exceeds the cost of re-acquiring from the world, but that cost is inferred from the choices and never measured or modelled, and the evidence is one task with small samples (seven subjects for the main data, three for the colour-change experiment) and no statistics reported in the article. What is left in the world is unprocessed input, not a computed result, and the article argues against precomputation where the needed products cannot be foreseen. | Active — read in full 2026-10-15 (the target article, pp. 723–742; the open peer commentaries and the authors' response, pp. 742–767, not read) from the typeset BBS PDF posted on Dana Ballard's University of Texas page (www.cs.utexas.edu/~dana/bbs.pdf; the same file is on Rajesh Rao's University of Washington page). Unpaywall and OpenAlex report the DOI closed. Worth reading as the founding statement of fixation as a pointer that binds a program variable to a place in the world at about a third of a second, and for the block-copying evidence that people re-look rather than memorize: about 1.3 looks at the model per block, the slowest lowest-memory strategy (about 3 s a block, against 1.5 s from memory) chosen most often under instructions to be fast, falling to 1.0 when looking is made dearer (70° separation) and 0.7 when patterns can be chunked. For [QUESTION-095](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-095.md) it shows the trade stated as a cost comparison ("carrying cost" of working memory against on-line acquisition) that moves with both costs, but the cost is inferred from choice, not measured or modelled, what is left in the world is raw input rather than a computed result, and the authors argue against precomputing where needs are unpredictable, so it is the deferral policy opposite to the cockpit's, not amortization; for [TERM-055](../../../record/terms.d/TERM-055.md) it shows people choosing between internal and external sources by their relative retrieval cost, and moving retrieval later, not earlier; for [CLAIM-298](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-298.md) it offers only an analogy (cue-driven matching, the same image read differently by task step) and no test of framing or judgement. |
| [LIT-1076](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1076.md) | The intelligent use of space | Kirsh (1995), Artificial Intelligence 73. A classification, from video of cooks, assemblers and baggers, informal observation and the Tetris studies, of how people arrange things around them to cut the time and memory a task needs: arrangements that simplify choice (hide or highlight affordances, eliminate decisions, offload heuristic properties), arrangements that simplify perception (clustering, regions, marking, the vernier effect), and spatial dynamics that save internal computation (Tetris rotation, self-cueing). It frames the savings in search-complexity terms and links informational structuring to amortized computation in a footnote, but says the savings cannot in general be meaningfully quantified and offers no cost model, no measurements beyond the cited Tetris timings, and no case of an arrangement failing under a deadline. Its agents are experts arranging their own workspace in the medium and short term; long-term, pre-built environments are set aside. | Active — read in full 2026-10-15 from the publisher's typeset article (Artificial Intelligence 73 (1995) 31–68), scanned and posted by the author on his UCSD pages (adrenaline.ucsd.edu/kirsh/Articles/Space/intelligent_useof_space.pdf), text taken by OCR, with the formulas checked against page images; his HTML pre-publication version on the same site was compared and differs in the footnotes and the Tetris timings. Worth reading as the standard classification of how people arrange their workspace to cut the time and memory a task needs: arrangements that simplify choice (hiding or highlighting affordances, eliminating decisions, heuristic cues), arrangements that simplify perception (clustering, regions, marking, the vernier effect) and spatial dynamics that save internal computation (Tetris rotation). It is drawn from observation and anecdote, with no measurements of its own beyond the Tetris timings it cites, and it declines to quantify the savings. For [QUESTION-095](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-095.md) it shows that the link from informational structuring to amortized computation was drawn in 1995, in a footnote to Tarjan and in §3.4's "set-up costs could be amortized over the whole task", but as an analogy to self-adjusting structures, not to memoization. It also shows that its third category, just-in-time offloading, is not amortization at all. For [CASE-085](../../../record/cases.d/CASE-085.md) and [TERM-055](../../../record/terms.d/TERM-055.md) it supports the gap between presence and finding in time: memory for location is "regularly overestimated", a meaningful pre-existing layout helps recall, and retrieval cost matters "in absolute time" even where it is a constant factor. It does not cover pre-built environments arranged by someone other than the retriever, or failures under a deadline. |
